nutshell: Event cameras were thought privacy-preserving since they don't capture RGB detail, but deep event-to-image reconstruction (E2VID) can recover identifiable grayscale images from event streams. This paper trains an event-stream anonymization network end-to-end against a frozen pretrained reconstruction attacker (to degrade its output) while jointly training a person-ReID head on the same anonymized events, and introduces the first real event-camera person-ReID dataset (Event-ReId) to evaluate it.
contributions: An end-to-end jointly-trained pipeline with three modules - an anonymization autoencoder (Ean), a frozen pretrained E2VID reconstruction network playing the privacy attacker (Erec), and a ReID backbone (Ereid) - optimized with a 3-term loss: a structural loss keeping the anonymized voxel grid usable for ReID, a reconstruction loss maximized to degrade the attacker's recovered image quality (SSIM), and an identity loss for ReID.

The first real event-camera person-ReID dataset, Event-ReId: 33 subjects captured across 4 synchronized event+RGB camera pairs (~4 sec streams each), with manual person/face bounding-box annotations and 9 of 33 subjects wearing face masks, released publicly on Zenodo.

Evaluates privacy not just via reconstructed-image quality (SSIM/PSNR) but via two downstream attack proxies - image retrieval with a SOTA ReID model (BoT) and face verification (ArcFace AUC) - plus an explicit inversion-attack test where a second network is trained specifically to reverse the anonymization.

Shows the learned anonymization simultaneously beats a prior hand-crafted event-encryption baseline (Du et al.) on privacy (lower SSIM/PSNR, near-random retrieval) and on retained ReID accuracy, unlike encryption which can't run downstream tasks directly on its encrypted output.
deficiencies: The inversion-attack test only trains the attacking network against paired data from this exact fixed anonymization network - a fairly favorable (near white-box) setup for the defender - so 'robust to this specific reconstruction pipeline and this specific inversion attacker' is a narrower claim than 'privacy-preserving' in general; a differently-designed or adaptively-trained attacker is never tested.

Both evaluation datasets are small and reported as single-split numbers with no repeated runs or confidence intervals: Event-ReId has only 33 subjects (22 train/11 test), and the SoftBio simulated split is 76/76 identities - the reported ~3.5-4.5 point Rank-1 privacy/utility trade-off rests on one test split each.

The comparison against the prior event-encryption baseline (Table 3) uses only 75% partial encryption for that method, chosen because full encryption reportedly destroys downstream-task usability entirely - the baseline isn't tuned to its own best usable operating point, so the head-to-head comparison may favor this paper's method by construction.

The privacy evaluation via image retrieval treats a near-random retrieval score as evidence of success, but there's no disentangled test showing the anonymization specifically targets identity-relevant information rather than just degrading general image quality/structure - the structural loss is validated on the ReID-utility side but not symmetrically checked on the privacy side.
notable: The loss ablation (Table 5) exposes a genuine, quantified privacy-utility trade-off worth citing directly rather than the paper's own softer framing of 'a small drop in performance': removing the structural loss entirely still anonymizes but drops Rank-1 from 63.7% to 54.5%, and adding it back only partially recovers to 59.2% - i.e., there's a real Pareto frontier here, not just a minor utility cost. Also notable: the released Event-ReId dataset deliberately includes 9 of 33 subjects wearing face masks, a useful stress-test for face-based re-identification robustness that the main results section doesn't otherwise analyze separately.
